expectedText:
CALIFORNIA RECORDING ACT AND PRIORITY OF INTERESTS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Taylor Morgan

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet explains California's real property recording system: the statutes that let a person put the county's public record on notice of an interest in real property, and the rule those statutes use to decide which of two competing claims to the same real property has priority when both cannot be honored in full. It is prepared in connection with real property located at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, more particularly described as Lot 12, Block 3, Tract No. 4567, as per map recorded in Book 45, Page 12 of Maps, Sacramento County Records, Assessor's Parcel Number 123-456-789, in San Francisco County. It is prepared for Jordan Alex Lee, in connection with an interest in that property also claimed by Taylor Morgan. This sheet describes California's recording statutes and how California courts have construed them. It does not determine who holds superior title to this specific property, does not itself record, correct, or clear any instrument affecting title, and is not a substitute for a professional title search, a policy of title insurance, or a quiet title action.

THE CORE PRIORITY RULE: CIVIL CODE SECTION 1214
California Civil Code section 1214 supplies the statutory rule that decides priority between competing claims to the same real property, such as an interest in 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield. Under that section, a conveyance of real property is void against a later purchaser or mortgagee of the same property who takes in good faith, pays valuable consideration, and is the first of the two to duly record — even if that later purchaser's own interest was actually created after the earlier, unrecorded (or later-recorded) one. California courts have described this as a "race-notice" framework: a subsequent purchaser obtains priority only by combining three things — good-faith, paid-for status without notice of the earlier interest; the fact that the earlier interest was in place before the subsequent purchaser acquired its own interest; and being the first of the two to duly record.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein, other than a lease for a term not exceeding one year, is void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee of the same property, or any part thereof, in good faith and for a valuable consideration, whose conveyance is first duly recorded, and as against any judgment affecting the title, unless the conveyance shall have been duly recorded prior to the record of notice of action."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1214 (California Legislative Information text), the race-notice recording-priority rule for real property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1214.)
  "Under these "race-notice" rules, a subsequent purchaser obtains priority for a real property interest by (1) acquiring the interest as a bona fide purchaser for valuable consideration with neither actual knowledge nor constructive notice of (2) a previously created interest and (3) "first duly record[ing]" the interest, i.e., recording before the previously created interest is recorded."
  — First Bank v. East West Bank, 199 Cal. App. 4th 1309, 1313-1314 (2011) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810622/first-bank-v-east-west-bank/)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own recording-priority rule for real property — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel or transfer, and not a determination of whether the person this sheet is prepared for, or the other claimant it names, in fact qualifies as the protected "subsequent purchaser or mortgagee" or holds the earlier interest on the facts of any specific dispute. The statutory quote and the case-law quote are independent sources — one is the Legislature's text, the other is a Court of Appeal's construction of it in a specific dispute over lien priority between two lenders — but the case does not carry the force of a statute and could in principle be narrowed or distinguished by a later decision. This clause states the general rule and its three-part structure only; it does not address what counts as "good faith" or "notice" for these purposes (addressed in a separate clause of this sheet) or how the rule applies when two conveyances are recorded at literally the same moment.

WHAT RECORDING DOES: CONSTRUCTIVE NOTICE UNDER CIVIL CODE SECTION 1213
Civil Code section 1213 states what recording accomplishes: once a conveyance of real property is acknowledged (or proved), certified, and recorded as prescribed by law, it becomes constructive notice of its contents to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees, from the time it is filed with the county recorder for record. "Constructive notice" in this context is a legal presumption, not a factual finding about who actually read the county's records — the law treats a later purchaser or mortgagee as bound by a properly recorded document's contents whether or not that person actually saw it. California courts have also construed the phrase "recorded as prescribed by law" to require more than the physical act of depositing a document with the recorder: the document must also be indexed, since it is the indexing — not the recording alone — that makes a document findable through a search of the public record and that triggers constructive notice.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein acknowledged or proved and certified and recorded as prescribed by law from the time it is filed with the recorder for record is constructive notice of the contents thereof to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees; and a certified copy of such a recorded conveyance may be recorded in any other county and when so recorded the record thereof shall have the same force and effect as though it was of the original conveyance and where the original conveyance has been recorded in any county wherein the property therein mentioned is not situated a certified copy of the recorded conveyance may be recorded in the county where such property is situated with the same force and effect as if the original conveyance had been recorded in that county."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1213 (California Legislative Information text), recording as constructive notice to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1213.)
  "The recording of a document does not impart constructive notice; "[t]he operative event [for purposes of constructive notice] is actually the indexing of the document . . . .""
  — First Bank v. East West Bank, 199 Cal. App. 4th 1309, 1315 (2011) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810622/first-bank-v-east-west-bank/)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute plus one Court of Appeal's construction of it — genuinely independent sources, since one is legislative text and the other is a judicial gloss reached in an unrelated dispute over the priority of two lenders' recorded trust deeds. This clause does not address the mechanics of how a particular county recorder's office indexes documents, how quickly indexing typically follows recording, or what happens if an indexing error occurs; those questions were not independently verified here. It also does not resolve whether the recording of any specific instrument affecting the property this sheet identifies was in fact properly acknowledged, certified, and indexed as section 1213 requires — that is a factual question about the specific instrument and county record, not something this sheet determines.

AN UNRECORDED INSTRUMENT'S EFFECT: CIVIL CODE SECTION 1217
Civil Code section 1217 states the flip side of the recording system: an unrecorded instrument affecting real property is not void or ineffective just because it was never recorded. It remains valid as between the original parties to it, and as against anyone else who has notice of it. What an unrecorded instrument cannot do is defeat the specific, protected category of later claimant described elsewhere in this sheet — a subsequent purchaser or mortgagee of the same property who takes in good faith, for valuable consideration, and records first. Read together, sections 1214 and 1217 describe the same underlying rule from two directions: section 1214 states when an earlier conveyance is cut off, and section 1217 confirms that outside that specific situation, an unrecorded instrument keeps its full effect.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An unrecorded instrument is valid as between the parties thereto and those who have notice thereof."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1217 (California Legislative Information text), an unrecorded instrument remains valid between the parties and anyone with notice of it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1217.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what an unrecorded instrument does and does not do under California law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel or instrument. Section 1217 is presented here on its own as a single statutory section; this sheet's companion clause on section 1214 is not offered as a second independent source for the point made in this clause specifically, since section 1217's function is largely to restate, from the opposite direction, the same priority rule section 1214 states directly — the two sections are not independent of one another on that shared point, even though each is separately numbered and separately quoted. This same section is also cited, for narrower purposes tied to a specific type of transfer, in other documents in this collection (a deed conveying property into a trust, for example); this sheet cites it instead for the general recording-system rule itself. This clause does not address what counts as "notice" sufficient to bind someone other than the original parties — that is addressed in a separate clause of this sheet.

WHAT "GOOD FAITH" AND "NOTICE" MEAN: HOW CALIFORNIA COURTS HAVE CONSTRUED THESE TERMS
Neither section 1214 nor section 1213 defines "good faith" or "notice" in detail; California courts have filled in those terms. A California Court of Appeal has described the elements a subsequent purchaser or mortgagee must show to qualify for section 1214's protection as payment of value, good faith, and the absence of actual or constructive notice of the earlier claimant's rights — the absence of notice being treated as an essential requirement, not merely one relevant factor among others. Separately, another Court of Appeal has explained that notice under these statutes can be actual (express information of a fact) or constructive (notice the law imputes regardless of what a person actually knew), and that a person generally has "notice" of a particular fact if that person has knowledge of circumstances which, upon reasonable inquiry, would lead to that particular fact.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The elements of bona fide purchase are payment of value, in good faith, and without actual or constructive notice of another's rights."
  — First Bank v. East West Bank, 199 Cal. App. 4th 1309, 1314 (2011), quoting Gates Rubber Co. v. Ulman, 214 Cal. App. 3d 356, 364 (1989) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810622/first-bank-v-east-west-bank/)
  "By statute, notice may be actual or constructive. Actual notice is defined as "express information of a fact," while constructive notice is that "which is imputed by law." ... A person generally has "notice" of a particular fact if that person has knowledge of circumstances which, upon reasonable inquiry, would lead to that particular fact."
  — Gregg v. Cloney, 91 Cal. App. 4th 429, 436-437 (2001) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5808717/gregg-v-cloney/)
  Known gap: This clause rests on two separately decided California Courts of Appeal opinions — First Bank v. East West Bank (2011) and Gregg v. Cloney (2001) — genuinely independent of one another, though both apply the same statutory scheme (Civil Code §§ 1213-1214) and neither is a decision of the California Supreme Court, so neither is binding on every California trial or appellate court and either could in principle be distinguished or narrowed by a later decision. First Bank v. East West Bank is also cited elsewhere in this sheet, for two different, more specific propositions (the overall race-notice framework, and the indexing requirement for constructive notice); it is not counted as a second independent source within those other clauses. This clause does not resolve what "reasonable inquiry" requires on any particular set of facts, does not address whether knowledge held by a purchaser's agent (such as an escrow officer or title company) can be imputed to the purchaser, and does not determine whether either party this sheet identifies in fact had, or lacked, notice of the other's competing claim to the property — those are fact-specific questions this sheet does not resolve.

DECLARANT ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Jordan Alex Lee acknowledges having reviewed this information sheet regarding California's recording act and the recording-priority rule for real property located at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield. This sheet was reviewed on September 1, 2026, in Sacramento, California.

_____________________________
Jordan Alex Lee
